title: Losing the Jarland Park job and Dodo's explanation
summary: He was passed over for an older man; the clarinetist Dodo later told him that he looked awkward playing left-handed.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And so I mean it was just one of those things that you figured I was just almost set for that because he was trying to get a bunch of the New Orleans playing musicians and whatnot. So at the last minute I was nixed out from this job. All my friends, it was quite embarrassing to me and everything, two or three of my real close boys that we'd come all up with, and we played about the same amount of music and everything. And he got a much older man who until this day at that time I know that I was more qualified for the job for what he was playing than this man was. So that just sort of broke my heart, you know, I just couldn't understand it. So one day about three weeks later, after they had opened on the job and everything was going very good, I ran into the clarinet player in the band who was a New Orleans boy, Dodo. He was a terrific clarinetist. Oh, I don't know him.
What was his last name? That's all I remember about Dodo.

He was terrific. One of the greatest of the old school clarinetists. So I ran into him on the streets and he started talking to me. And he just put it right on the line. He said, you know why you lost that job, why you didn't get that job. He went on to explain, he said, your playing would fit right in the front of me doing. I mean, you fit there, you belong there. He said, the man that we have, he don't play near as much as you playing. He don't fit. He said, but they say that you look awkward on the stands. They look like you're playing your instrument backwards. He said, it looks bad. As far as your actual playing and your musical ability, everything was all right. But they said, just look bad. So he gave me some advice. He said, the first chance you get, if I was you, I would turn that instrument around and start playing it right hand. And then, there's no excuse in it. So, that thing, it sunk in.
